title: The Boy Who Built a Voice

pages.text: When fifteen-year-old Elorm joined the school's robotics club, everyone wanted to meet him. He enjoyed drawing, mathematics and solving puzzles. But speaking was difficult for him. Sometimes he used gestures. Sometimes he typed words on a tablet. A boy named Kobby spoke loudly. "Can he understand us?" Elorm raised an eyebrow, typed a sentence and pressed the tablet's speaker. "Of course I can. I am standing right here." The room went silent. Then Elorm smiled. Kobby blushed. "Sorry."

pages.alt: Fifteen-year-old Elorm smiling in the robotics club after using his tablet speaker to reply to Kobby.

pages.text: During a club meeting, the teacher asked everyone to identify a problem technology might help solve. Kobby thought about Elorm's tablet. "Could we build a communication tool that works well with Ghanaian names and everyday expressions?" Elorm typed: "Perhaps. But ask people who use these tools what they actually need." Kobby nodded. "Would you help us design it?" Elorm grinned. "Only if you promise not to make all the decisions for me." "Deal!"

pages.text: The students created a simple application with large buttons. One button said, "Good morning." Another said, "Please give me a moment." A third said, "I would like to ask a question." The application converted selected text into speech. Kobby pressed the first button. The computer spoke in a strange, hurried voice. Everyone laughed. Then Elorm typed: "Funny voice. Useful idea. More work needed." Their teacher nodded. "That is what prototypes are for."

pages.text: The students tested the application with several Ghanaian names. Some pronunciations sounded wrong. Elorm shook his head. "People's names matter." Kobby agreed. They began collecting pronunciation examples from volunteers who had given permission. They learned that speech technology could make mistakes, especially when its training and testing did not adequately represent the people using it. "Then good technology needs good data," Kobby said. "And respectful testing," Elorm added.

pages.text: One afternoon, a club member suggested recording every conversation automatically. "That will give us more data!" Elorm's expression changed. He typed: "Would you want someone recording you without asking?" The room became quiet. Their teacher explained that collecting voices and personal information required care, permission, security and appropriate safeguards. The students changed their design. The application would not secretly record conversations. They also planned ways to minimize unnecessary data collection.

pages.text: At the school technology exhibition, Kobby proudly introduced the application. Then the internet connection failed. The demonstration stopped. Kobby stared at the screen. "Oh no." Elorm calmly opened an offline communication board they had prepared. He selected a message. "Technology should work for people, even when things go wrong." The visitors applauded. Kobby realized that reliability and accessibility were just as important as impressive features.

pages.text: A local technology entrepreneur visited the club. "Could this become a business?" she asked. "Yes!" Kobby replied. "Who are your users? How will you maintain the software? What will it cost? How will you protect their data? Can people afford it?" Kobby hesitated. Elorm typed: "We need to research those questions before promising anything." The entrepreneur smiled. "That is a good beginning." She encouraged the students to seek guidance from people with disabilities, educators, developers and accessibility specialists.

pages.text: Months later, the students demonstrated an improved prototype. It offered customizable phrases, offline features and more careful pronunciation options. Elorm tested it. The tablet spoke: "I have something important to say." He paused. Then he typed another sentence. "Actually, I have many important things to say." Everyone laughed. Kobby smiled. "The technology did not give you ideas." "No," Elorm typed. "It helps me express them."

pages.text: At the end of the school year, the robotics club received an invitation to present its project at a student innovation exhibition. Kobby looked at Elorm. "Do you think we could build something used across Ghana?" Elorm typed: "Maybe. But first, we should make it genuinely useful for the people who need it." Kobby nodded. They had started with the dream of building a clever machine. They had discovered something more important. The best inventions begin by listening to people.

activities.question: Why did the application mispronounce some Ghanaian names?
options: Better testing and suitable pronunciation data were needed.
The tablet battery was completely empty.
Ghanaian names cannot be spoken aloud.
activities.explanation: Its pronunciation system did not handle those names accurately; better testing and suitable pronunciation information were needed.

activities.question: What does text-to-speech software do?
options: Converts written text into spoken audio
Secretly records every conversation in a room
Repairs broken internet cables automatically
activities.explanation: Text-to-speech software converts written text into spoken audio.

activities.question: Why should users help design assistive technology?
options: They understand their own needs and preferences.
Users should never be consulted during design.
Developers already know what everyone wants without asking.
activities.explanation: People who use assistive tools understand their own lived needs and preferences best.

activities.question: Should the application record people without permission?
options: No; collecting voices requires permission and safeguards.
Yes; secret recording is the best way to gather data.
Yes; privacy rules do not apply to student clubs.
activities.explanation: No. Collecting voices and personal information requires care, permission, security and safeguards.

activities.question: Why are offline features useful in an assistive communication app?
options: They keep essential functions available without internet.
They make the tablet heavier to carry.
They prevent users from customizing phrases.
activities.explanation: Offline features help keep essential communication functions available even when internet connections fail.

activities.question: Which questions should a founder answer before launching a product?
options: User needs, costs, affordability, maintenance and privacy
Only what colour shirt to wear at the exhibition
How to promise features before researching them
activities.explanation: Founders must research user needs, maintenance, costs, affordability, privacy and accessibility before making promises.

activities.prompt: If you sketch an accessible feature for a school app, what makes your design effective?
options: A practical design that addresses a real user need
A complicated screen that requires fast internet at all times
A feature built without asking any users for feedback

glossary.definition: Movements of the hands, head or body used to express meaning or communicate.
An early working model of a product built to test an idea and learn what needs improvement.
The ways in which words or names are spoken aloud.
Protective rules and technical measures that keep people and their personal data safe.
The quality of working dependably and consistently, even in difficult conditions.
Designing products and environments so that people with diverse abilities can use them effectively.
Able to be adjusted or modified to suit a particular user’s needs and preferences.
